reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A state of profound reduction in spontaneous movement and speech despite preserved wakefulness and the apparent capacity to move and speak
The patient may appear alert with eyes open and visually track the examiner, yet initiate little or no purposeful activity (coma vigil)
Represents the extreme end of the abulia spectrum, reflecting a disorder of drive and initiation rather than of motor or language pathways themselves

The mesial frontal form follows bilateral damage to the anterior cingulate and supplementary motor areas, often from anterior cerebral artery infarction or ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm
A paramedian (diencephalic-midbrain) form results from lesions of the paramedian thalamus and upper midbrain reticular structures
Causes include stroke, hydrocephalus, trauma, tumour, hypoxic injury, and infective or inflammatory disease
Management targets the underlying cause, with dopaminergic agents sometimes used to improve drive and initiation
reference.pathophysiology: Akinetic mutism results from disruption of the networks that generate motivation and initiate goal-directed behaviour, sparing the primary motor and language systems. The mesial frontal form involves bilateral injury to the anterior cingulate cortex and supplementary motor area, key hubs linking limbic drive to motor action, commonly from anterior cerebral artery territory infarction or anterior communicating artery aneurysm rupture. The paramedian form arises from lesions of the paramedian thalamus and rostral midbrain, disrupting ascending activating and dopaminergic projections that energise cortical activity. In both, dopaminergic mesocortical and frontal-subcortical circuit dysfunction leaves the patient awake but lacking the internal drive to move or speak, which underlies the occasional benefit of dopaminergic therapy.
additionalDifferentials: Persistent vegetative or minimally conscious state
Advanced parkinsonism or other hypokinetic disorder
additionalInvestigations: MRI brain to localise mesial frontal, paramedian thalamic, or midbrain lesions
Vascular imaging for anterior cerebral or communicating artery pathology
Electroencephalography to exclude non-convulsive status epilepticus and assess arousal
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis where infection or inflammation is suspected
Assessment for hydrocephalus with consideration of shunting
redFlags: Acute deterioration suggesting new infarction, haemorrhage, or hydrocephalus
Fever or meningism indicating an infective or inflammatory cause
Findings suggesting an alternative reversible cause such as seizures
reference.prognosis: Recovery varies widely with cause and lesion extent; some patients improve substantially, particularly when a treatable cause such as hydrocephalus is corrected or with dopaminergic therapy, whereas extensive bilateral injury may leave a persistent deficit.
pitfalls: Mistaking the state for coma, vegetative state, or locked-in syndrome
Attributing the presentation to depression and missing a structural lesion
Overlooking non-convulsive status epilepticus as a reversible cause
Not trialling dopaminergic therapy where appropriate
